title: Supercharge Android media experiences with Jetpack Media3 and CameraX

segments.text: [MUSIC PLAYING]
BASSAM DGHEIM: Hi, everyone.
Welcome to our technical session on supercharging your Android
media experiences.
I'm Bassam, a product manager for Android Camera and Media.
Joining me today are Nevin from developer relations
and Kailiang from our engineering team.
We're thrilled to show you how Android
is evolving to help you build more engaging experiences
for our users.
Let's get started.
Our relationship with media has fundamentally changed.
It's no longer something we just consume.
It's how we create, how we connect, and how we live.
More and more, we see how media is a vital element of Android.
And as that relationship evolves,
we also see that our users are deeply engaged with their media
as they use their devices to watch, listen, create, share,
and connect.
This is why we want your media to feel effortless.
Every video you watch, every song you hear,
and every story you love should be
delivered with brilliant, uninterrupted quality.
With that comes a promise to also be your creative partner,
making it simple to capture your life as you remember it
and craft the stories only you can tell.
We strive to deliver media that you don't just see
but you can step inside.
To deliver on that vision, we are focusing our investments
across key, high impact areas.
First, we are continuing investments heavily
into quality, power, and performance, ensuring
ExoPlayer helps you deliver the most power efficient media
experience on Android that is consistent, reliable,
and lag-free.
We're also focusing on end-to-end creator journeys,
enabling applications to take advantage of our leading edge
intelligent camera with our seamless
CameraX toolkit and Media3 editing
libraries that unlock magical experiences for our most
creative users.
Finally, we are investing in immersive experiences
our users can feel.
As content breaks free from the flat screen,
we are building the definitive platform for spatial media.
Using our open source Eclipse engine,
we will enable you to capture and playback spatial content
on your Android devices.
As we build on our core investments,
we are proud of the innovative features we
have brought to the ecosystem.
Working really closely with partners like Meta,
we've been able to bring experiences like Low Light Boost
to the hands of many users.
We're also bringing more innovative AI features
like Magic Eraser and Studio Sound to the platform
to enable the most creative users to have the tools
to express themselves freely.
Besides all the experiences we are enabling,
we're incredibly proud to see continued adoption
of our Jetpack libraries.
We'll share more on how these libraries can
help you take advantage of the latest camera
and media features on Android throughout this talk.
To dive into the details, I'll pass it off
to Kailiang and Nevin.
NEVIN MITAL: Thanks, Bassam.
When we talk about being able to capture in any scenario,
we mean giving your users the power
to grab the perfect shot every time without friction.
We're committed to bridging the gap between system capabilities
and in-app features with CameraX.
CameraX abstracts away the complexities of the underlying
camera hardware, providing a consistent and powerful API
surface.
Let's look at what's new.
For example, starting with version 1.5 of CameraX,
you can capture uncompressed, unprocessed DNG images
for maximum creative flexibility for pro-level editing.
On the video front, we've introduced
a widely anticipated feature, High Frame Rate Capture.
You can capture fast moving action at high frame rates
and encode it as is for exceptionally smooth video
or directly encode it at a lower frame rate
for dramatic slow motion video.
For code samples and details on device compatibility
and limitations, check out our blog post for this feature.
Modern camera experiences will often combine multiple features,
but how do you know if a device supports HDR video, and 60
frames per second, and preview stabilization
all at the same time?
The new feature group API in CameraX removes the guesswork.
The feature group API currently supports HLG 10 HDR video,
60 frames per second, preview stabilization,
and ultra HDR image.
You can provide a prioritized list of features
and CameraX will determine the best combination supported
by the device, enabling them in order of your list.
You might consider using this API to create a settings
UI that disables toggles for unsupported options.
For more guidance, visit our feature group blog post.
Moving on, next, let's take a look at Low Light Boost,
a powerful feature for brightening the camera
stream in real time for previews and recordings.
Instagram recently added support for Low Light Boost
to help users capture memories at night
with as much authentic detail as possible.
With CameraX, implementing the hardware
accelerated AE mode of Low Light Boost in your capture flow
takes just a single line, calling the CameraControl.En
ableLowLightBoost AsyncAPI.
Check out our developer documentation for guidance
on how to enable the software implementation of Low Light
Boost as a fallback solution on devices where Low Light Boost AE
mode isn't available.
So far, we've covered how CameraX can adapt your capture
experiences to different environments,
from fast action to low light.
But users also have a variety of devices
now, including foldables, tablets, headsets, and glasses.
So it's more important than ever to build
a camera experience that can seamlessly
adapt to new form factors.
Here's Kailiang to show you how.
KAILIANG CHEN: CameraX already included
tools you need to build adaptive capture experiences that
enable users to make the most of their devices.
Make sure to use the CameraX Viewfinder
Composable to automatically manage reconfigurations, aspect
ratios, and scaling to prevent stretches or stuttering
previews.
This works out of the box, saving you
from writing device-specific workarounds.
Here I have some sample CameraX code for setting up
a preview use previous case.
And it's important that we store the surface request from CameraX
as a state in our ViewModel.
We can then pass the surface request into CameraX Viewfinder
and it will handle lifecycle management recomposition
as needed.
While we're on the topic of helping
users make the most of their devices, here's something cool.
We can use the JPEG Picture-in-picture library
to give users the ability to multitask
while recording with CameraX.
Going back to our Camera Viewfinder example,
we'll add an instance of basic picture-in-picture
from the JPEG Picture-in-picture library.
We'll also create a function that
updates the picture-in-picture params based
on where our camera preview is positioned on the screen.
And finally, in our CameraX Viewfinder,
we will call updateSourceRectHint
when it gets positioned.
Now whenever we want to enable this,
we simply call Enter Picture-in-picture mode
on this activity.
NEVIN MITAL: For example, this might
be useful for reading a script while recording.
KAILIANG CHEN: And finally, looking ahead,
CameraX is at the forefront of new format
support with the addition of Motion Photo.
Later this year, you'll be able to use CameraX to implement
motion photo capture capabilities in your app, which
are already supported for editing and playback
in JPEG Media3.
NEVIN MITAL: Speaking of editing,
next we'll show how the transformer APIs in Jetpack
Media3 are designed to make creative and complex editing
easy.
A major focus for Transformer has
been to enable more complex editing workflows.
And the APIs now have support for multi-asset editing.
Multi-asset editing refers to the suite
of tools necessary to composite multiple input media items
into a single output video.
This could include, for example, concatenating
items one after the other, overlaying them, or arranging
them for simultaneous playback, and applying operations
that span multiple items.
In Media3, you can apply effects and transformations
to media with the Effects API, preview the fully composited
compositions with Composition Player,
and finally, export the creation to an output
video with Transformer.
To apply effects to a single media item,
you can create an edited media item,
which groups a media item with a list
of video effects and audio processors to apply to it.
You can arrange multiple edited media
item instances into an edited media item sequence and layer
multiple edited media item sequences together
into a composition.
There are some editing options, like HDR behavior, that you can
apply at the composition level.
You can then play this composition with a composition
player to preview your edits or pass the composition
into an instance of transformer to export
a video with the edits baked in.
On top of this, Transformer is packed with new features
and improvements, including faster trimming with Edit List
Metadata so you can quickly create high quality, shortened
video clips by marking the start and stop boundaries using
metadata instead of re-encoding the clip;
new input format support, such as Android Professional
Video for professional grade editing control;
Media3 Muxer as the default rather than the platform
muxer for more consistent behavior across devices;
and a more intuitive API for speed adjustment and frame
rate setting as part of the Edited Media Item Builder.
One developer taking advantage of Transformer is Adobe.
For their upcoming Adobe Premiere app,
Adobe used Transformer as the foundation of their media
editing infrastructure to reduce their maintenance costs
and ensure greater compatibility across the Android ecosystem
while maintaining the flexibility they
need to use their own custom graphics pipeline.
Beyond Transformer, to help tackle video encoder
fragmentation across the diverse Android ecosystem,
we're also introducing the new Codec DB module in Media3.
This project leverages extensive testing from real devices
to provide data-driven, chipset-specific recommendations
for optimal video encoder settings.
You can use Codec DB's recommendations
to achieve better and more consistent
video quality across devices at a target bit rate,
all while avoiding device-specific issues.
Here's an example where we've encoded a video with default
settings on the left and with Codec DB's provided settings
on the right.
See if you can notice the improvement that Codec DB's
recommendations have had.
We can look at a single frame for side by side comparison.
Notice the reduced blurriness in the branches of the bush,
the sharper lines in the building,
and the clear delineation between the mountain
and the sky.
With Codec DB, the API is designed for you
to express an intent rather than a granular configuration.
In this example, we're optimizing for high quality
recording, but could instead request settings for use cases
like live streaming or social media posting.
We can also outline any constraints we're aware of.
For example, the video resolution,
specific codecs to consider, and a target quality level.
And if, by chance, Codec DB doesn't
have the data needed to provide a recommendation,
we can also define a fallback configuration.
At time of recording, the API is still actively in development,
so please refer to the latest documentation
for up-to-date guidance.
KAILIANG CHEN: Looking ahead, we're
also developing advanced on-device AI-powered effects
to help redefine mobile storytelling for users
and empower developers to ship premium AI-driven experiences
across Android ecosystem.
The first of these features that we're excited to introduce
is image and video enhanced.
This model includes tone mapping, denoising, deblurring,
and super resolution capabilities.
This can be valuable, for example,
by enabling you to deliver smaller or low quality
media to save on storage and bandwidth costs,
and still restore image and video to high quality
at the time of delivery.
We've been partnering with Instagram Edits app
to test this feature and will be rolling it out soon.
To give users more creative control,
we're also eager to bring Magic Eraser capability to apps
through these effects.
Magic Eraser leverages on-device models
to intelligently remove unwanted objects or distractions
from the picture and fill in the background.
And finally, to enable clearer and more professional audio
in videos, we are launching Studio Sound.
This is an AI-empowered feature designed
to improve audio quality by distinguishing
between different audio sources like speech, music,
and background noise.
Users can then reduce distraction
and boost the key sounds.
I will pause here for a moment so you
can hear the difference creators can make with this feature.
[VIDEO PLAYBACK]
- Baby, please don't cry.
We're cutting for your dinner.
Baby please don't cry.
We're cutting for your dinner.
[END PLAYBACK]
KAILIANG CHEN: To make it straightforward
for you to access these new capabilities and more,
we are delivering them through a standard interface
in a new Media3 AI Effects Library.
That means you can adopt a feature once
and we'll take care of all the heavy lifting
to dynamically use the optimal implementations at runtime based
on device capabilities.
This is helpful because this feature
can come from different sources to take
maximum advantage of software and hardware they run on.
For example, they could be implemented
in software for broad reach.
They could be released as a new feature in Android platform
for deeper system integrations, or they
could be a hardware accelerator model for optimized performance.
The new AI Effects Module in JPEG Media3
will abstract away this complexity
so you automatically get the best experience, even on devices
update to provide more optimized paths.
This framework is a powerful and extensible interface
that enables you to stay on the cutting edge
and adopt the latest advances for Google research
with minimal effort.
We are excited to bring these advanced capabilities
to your apps and eager to see the delightfully creative
experience you can craft with them.
Please stay tuned for an upcoming
release of JPEG Media3 library that includes these APIs.
NEVIN MITAL: Finally, let's talk about the last crucial piece,
playback.
Jetpack Media3's ExoPlayer is the recommended solution
for media playback in Android apps.
And we continue to invest heavily
in making it more efficient, reliable, and feature rich.
Let's run rapid fire through some of these improvements.
KAILIANG CHEN: We've heard your feedback on improving the user
experience during seeking.
ExoPlayer now has a new scrubbing mode.
Enable it via ExoPlayer dot setScrubbingModeEnabled.
This optimizes performance for frequent user-driven
seeks, like dragging a seek bar, resulting
in a much more smoother experience.
If you have a scrubbing UI, you should additionally configure
the seek tolerance values.
This allows ExoPlayer to be more efficient
decoding frames while seeking.
In this example, we are setting the tolerance to 8 DP
before and after the seeking position,
which allows ExoPlayer to find an optimal frame to seek to
within that range.
NEVIN MITAL: Last year, we announced the player surface
composable.
And we're continuing to add more Compose UI
elements to the library, including button and state
holders for playback controls like play,
next, mute, and shuffle; a state holder for playback progress
that can be used to create a progress indicator;
and content frame, a composable that helps handle scaling
and underlying player surface while maintaining its aspect
ratio and also has an easily enabled shutter
to hide the playback content.
We've also introduced the new UI Compose Material 3
module, which provides components
with Material 3 design styling.
This includes individual components
such as playback control buttons, position and duration
text, and a progress slider that allows seeking.
Here you can see the Media3 Compose demo
app, which uses the new top level player composable.
This provides a basic player UI layout with customizable slots
to add controls.
KAILIANG CHEN: Preloading content
is key to fast startup times, especially
for short form content.
We've enhanced our preload manager
with caching support and improved memory management.
NEVIN MITAL: We've also introduced new APIs
for frame and metadata extraction, which
have better reliability and format
support than the equivalent platform APIs.
KAILIANG CHEN: For remote playback,
Media3 now has enhanced cast support with the new cast player
API.
This player implementation acts as a drop-in replacement
to ExoPlayer for seamless transitions
between local and cast playback, handling the playback state
management on your behalf.
NEVIN MITAL: We're also happy to announce that Eclipsa Video is
launching on Android.
Eclipsa Video is a next generation HDR video format
that provides exceptional color and stunning imagery
across a diverse set of devices.
Android is the first operating system
to adopt this new standard.
Eclipsa Video removes a class of issues plaguing existing HDR
videos today, such as unpredictable light levels
and inconsistent rendering across devices.
We've updated ExoPlayer to provide out-of-the-box box
support for playback, so you can deliver high quality HDR videos
to your users with little to no effort.
KAILIANG CHEN: In addition, with how much
time users spend consuming media on their phones,
we are putting extra focus into power saving and reliability
for playback use cases.
And you can explore some of these work in progress
improvements in Media3 main branch, including PCM offload.
For apps with audio only, screen off playback use cases,
enabling PCM offload can result in up to 25% battery savings
based on our lab testing data.
Dynamic scheduling, which allows the CPU
to adapt how frequently it wakes up based on the workload.
Renderer pre-warming to efficiently prepare
resources needed for playback ahead of time
for lower start up latency.
Stack player detection to give remote signals
if the player ever gets stuck in buffering or playing state
without making progress, helping you identify and fix issues.
BASSAM DGHEIM: So to recap, Jetpack CameraX
helps you build powerful and consistent camera experiences
to capture in any scenario.
Media3 Transformer makes creative and complex editing
easy and performant.
And Media3 ExoPlayer delivers efficient and reliable playback.
KAILIANG CHEN: Exactly.
And together, they supercharge your Android media experiences.
NEVIN MITAL: We can't wait to see what you build.
For more information on anything we
covered, check out the latest documentation and samples linked
in the video description below.
[MUSIC PLAYING]
